Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I put on loud music or TV
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
People are not what they seem
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette: Maria, a 34-year-old Latina who works as a prison guard, first came to remember the day she fled from the northern border, a narrow river swollen by a sudden storm. She had been chased by armed soldiers, a sudden flash of gunfire and the bitter taste of gunpowder filling her lungs. The memory is so vivid that when she later hears the crackle of a radio transmission or the whir of a cell door, the sound feels like the gunfire itself. The day of escape left her convinced the world is a dangerous place, and that people in uniforms are not to be trusted. The sense of identity loss settled in her mind as the only thing that stayed was a fragment of her former self, the one who knew how to cook a quick tamale or laugh with her husband. The smell of alcohol in the break room at the prison office brings her back to that river in a single breath. As soon as the scent hits her nose, she starts to ruminate about how the escape could have been avoided, wondering if she should have left earlier. She also feels a sudden, almost reflexive need to put on a headset and blast loud music or switch on a television at maximum volume; it is her way of drowning out the phantom gunfire. The scent also triggers a false alarm - she flinches as if a bullet is about to strike - and she immediately chooses a seat near the back of the guard room, the one that feels most protected. In the same breath she looks away from the authority figures in uniform, convinced that their orders are a prelude to violence. Thus, each trigger is a spark that ignites her maladaptive strategies, feeds her threat monitoring, and deepens her belief that the world is unsafe. Her negative appraisals feed back into this loop. She believes that the world is dangerous, that people are not what they seem, and that she has lost a part of herself. These beliefs make her wary of authority; the very men who issue orders become triggers that pull her into avoidance. She feels compelled to keep away from those in uniform, a habit that extends into her nightly routines - she only goes out for dinner with her husband after midnight, when he has left the house. In that avoidance, she experiences a sense of isolation, reinforcing her distrust of others. The appraisal that the world is hostile also stokes her memories: whenever she hears a sound from the prison's corridors, she recalls the river's roar and feels overwhelmed, to the point that she stops and lies on the floor of the break room to regain composure. When the memory resurfaces, it brings with it a cascade of reactions. The auditory recall - the echo of gunfire - triggers a startle to movement, a sudden jump at the sight of a closing door. The memory is so vivid that she sees the river's rush again, and she feels the same cold fear. In response, she flinches, which in turn confirms her false alarms and intensifies her sense of threat. The memory also fuels her negative appraisals; the more she recalls, the more she believes the world is dangerous and that she has lost herself. The memory is the linchpin that pulls her into sensory distraction: she turns on the TV, listens to loud music, and tries to drown out the sounds that feel like gunfire. The threat that she experiences - false alarms, startled movement, the compulsive search for safe seats - keeps her in a constant state of alert. The threat heightens her memories; each time she perceives danger, she revisits the river, hearing the crackle of gunfire again. Each threat also feeds her negative appraisals; the more she believes she is in danger, the more she trusts that the world is hostile. Threat, in turn, acts as a trigger for her maladaptive strategies; when she feels threatened, she retreats to avoidance, listens to music, and ruminates on prevention. These strategies then reinforce her memories, her threat perception, and her negative appraisals, creating a tightening cycle that has taken hold of her work and home life. She has begun to miss work due to anxiety, and her husband has stopped visiting after she told him she could not trust the officers who run the facility. It is this relentless spiral that has driven Maria to seek help. The night she sat alone in her apartment, her hands trembling as she tried to listen to the muted television and she could not sleep, she realized that her fears were no longer just a part of her past-they were a part of her present, choking her ability to enjoy the life she once had. She is most afraid of being trapped in that river again, of losing her husband or of being alone in a world that she can no longer trust. Yet, amidst that fear, she holds a fragile hope that a new understanding could free her from the loop and allow her to see that she is still the woman who once could cook tamales and laugh, not just a survivor of a violent border crossing.
